sources.source: Structured Streaming Programming Guide: foreachBatch (Apache Spark docs)

items.item: foreachBatch provides only at-least-once write guarantees by default, but the batchId can be used to deduplicate the output and get an exactly-once guarantee
ON CONFLICT can be used to specify an alternative action to raising a unique constraint or exclusion constraint violation error

Advancing a checkpoint before writing the output loses the batch entirely on a crash between them, measured directly: the checkpoint is marked done, the crash happens before any output write, and nothing downstream ever retries a batch the checkpoint already calls finished.

Writing the output before advancing the checkpoint only duplicates a batch on restart, never loses it, because the rows were already durably written before the crash; committing both together as one atomic step stays consistent regardless of which side of the commit the crash lands on, all three orderings measured directly against the identical mock warehouse.

A batch id derived from the input range it covers computes to the identical value on every run of that same range, so a re-run overwrites the same destination; a batch id derived from a counter or the clock names a new destination each run, so a re-run's rows pile up beside the first attempt's — both measured directly across two full runs of the identical input.

items.item: At-least-once delivery (redeliveries allowed) plus an idempotent, keyed write (applying one twice is harmless) is the general recipe for an exactly-once effect, not exactly-once delivery; proved directly by crashing a batch partway through, re-running it to completion, and diffing the result byte for byte against a single clean run with no crash at all.

items.item: A crash that duplicates an entire batch produces rows that individually pass every row-level check, because each row is correct on its own — the bug is only visible at the level of how many times the batch as a whole was applied, not in any single row's contents.

The wrong half of the predict question — that writing the output first loses data because the checkpoint never catches up — is ruled out directly: a crash after the output write but before the checkpoint advance leaves the rows durably written, so a restart can only redo that work, never lose it.

A deterministic batch id and an idempotent write are two separate decisions that only together produce a safe re-run: a deterministic id without an idempotent write still produces a duplicate at the same destination if the write itself isn't keyed, and an idempotent write without a deterministic id never gets the chance to overwrite, because every re-run computes a new destination.

The byte-for-byte diff in the final measured reveal is checked against a second run that never crashed at all, not merely against the first attempt's own partial state — proving the recipe reaches the identical outcome as the no-failure case, not just a self-consistent one.

at.step: Reveal: proof by diffing two runs, measured
